title: Verifying Intent and Harm: A Unified Defense Against LLM-Generated Threats
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in interactive applications, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial interactions that induce harmful, deceptive, or policy-violating outputs. Existing defenses typically analyze either user prompts or generated outputs, but not both. However, many real-world attacks exploit a separation between adversarial intent expressed in the prompt and actionable harm manifested only in the response. As a result, prompt-only and response-only defenses frequently miss unsafe interactions that appear benign when viewed from either side in isolation. We present a verification-centric defense framework that jointly evaluates prompt intent and response harm before an LLM response is delivered to a user. The framework employs specialized analysts for intent and harm assessment together with a Judge for conflict resolution. We formalize a threat model for prompt-response attacks and evaluate the framework across five threat categories: jailbreaks, prompt injection, phishing, cyber abuse, and harmful content. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show that jointly verifying prompt intent and response harm consistently outperforms single-sided defenses and single-agent reasoning baselines. Across threat categories, the framework improves average F1 from 0.90 for the strongest applicable baselines to 0.95 while reducing the average attack success rate to 4.1 percent. Compared with a Single-Agent+CoT baseline, it improves average F1 from 0.87 to 0.95 and reduces the false positive rate on benign-sensitive requests from 0.12 to 0.06. We further evaluate architecture-aware adaptive attacks in which the attacker knows the verifier structure and attempts to bypass individual verification components. Our results suggest that prompt-response verification provides a practical foundation for securing LLM applications against evolving adversarial threats.

title: Error-Aware Policy Learning: Zero-Shot Generalization in Partially Observable Dynamic Environments
abstract: Simulation provides a safe and efficient way to generate useful data for learning complex robotic tasks. However, matching simulation and real-world dynamics can be quite challenging, especially for systems that have a large number of unobserved or unmeasurable parameters, which may lie in the robot dynamics itself or in the environment with which the robot interacts. We introduce a novel approach to tackle such a sim-to-real problem by developing policies capable of adapting to new environments, in a zero-shot manner. Key to our approach is an error-aware policy (EAP) that is explicitly made aware of the effect of unobservable factors during training. An EAP takes as input the predicted future state error in the target environment, which is provided by an error-prediction function, simultaneously trained with the EAP. We validate our approach on an assistive walking device trained to help the human user recover from external pushes. We show that a trained EAP for a hip-torque assistive device can be transferred to different human agents with unseen biomechanical characteristics. In addition, we show that our method can be applied to other standard RL control tasks.

title: ARYA: A Physics-Constrained Composable & Deterministic World Model Architecture
abstract: This paper presents ARYA, a composable, physics-constrained, deterministic world model architecture built on five foundational principles: nano models, composability, causal reasoning, determinism, and architectural AI safety. We demonstrate that ARYA satisfies all canonical world model requirements, including state representation, dynamic prediction, causal and physical awareness, temporal consistency, generalization, learnability, and planning and control. Unlike monolithic foundation models, the ARYA foundation model implements these capabilities through a hierarchical system-of-system-of-systems of specialized nano models, orchestrated by AARA (ARYA Autonomous Research Agent), an always-on cognitive daemon that executes a continuous sense-decide-act-learn loop. The nano model architecture provides linear scaling, sparse activation, selective untraining, and sub-20-second training cycles, resolving the traditional tension between capability and computational efficiency. A central contribution is the Unfireable Safety Kernel: an architecturally immutable safety boundary that cannot be disabled or circumvented by any system component, including its own self-improvement engine. This is not a social or ethical alignment statement; it is a technical framework ensuring human control persists as autonomy increases. Safety is an architectural constraint governing every operation, not a policy layer applied after the fact. We present formal alignment between ARYA's architecture and canonical world model requirements, and report summarizing its state-of-the-art performance across 6 of 9 competitive benchmarks head-to-head with GPT-5.2, Opus 4.6, and V-JEPA-2. All with zero neural network parameters, across seven active industry domain nodes spanning aerospace, pharma manufacturing, oil and gas, smart cities, biotech, defense, and medical devices.

title: DexHoldem: An Agentic Robotics Benchmark for Dexterous Manipulation in Texas Hold'em
abstract: Evaluating embodied systems with real dexterous hardware requires more than isolated motor-skill tests: an agent must perceive a changing scene (e.g. a tabletop), choose a context-appropriate action, execute it with a dexterous hand, and leave the scene usable for later decisions. We introduce DexHoldem, a comprehensive real-world benchmark evaluating Texas Hold'em related dexterous manipulations with a ShadowHand. DexHoldem provides 1,470 teleoperated demonstrations across 14 Texas Hold'em manipulation primitives, a standardized physical policy benchmark, and an agentic perception benchmark that tests whether agents can recover the structured game state needed for embodied decision making. On primitive execution, $π_{0.5}$ obtains the highest task completion rate ($61.2\%$), while $π_{0.5}$ and $π_0$ tie on scene-preserving success rate ($47.5\%$). On agentic perception, Opus 5.5 narrowly leads on both strict problem-level accuracy ($49.1\%$) and average field-wise accuracy ($80.6\%$); the gap between the two exposes the distance between isolated visual sub-capabilities and complete routing-relevant state recovery. Finally, we instantiate the full embodied-agent loop with one agent--policy pairing over 33 closed-loop hand-level rollouts, in which only $12.1\%$ of hands complete; retries restore the failed primitive in 12 of 34 dispatches and resolve prolonged execution stalls in three of the four completed hands, which would otherwise have required manual termination. Only one hand completes with neither a retry nor a human-help request. DexHoldem therefore evaluates dexterous tabletop execution, agentic perception, and embodied decision routing in a shared physical setting. Project website: https://dexholdem.github.io/Dexholdem/

title: Building the Truman Show: A TrustZone-Based Framework for Lightweight Out-of-band Kernel Security Monitoring
abstract: The increasing number of vulnerabilities in operating systems, together with sophisticated kernel-level threats (e.g., rootkits), has weakened the effectiveness of traditional in-kernel protection mechanisms. Since these defenses operate at the same privilege level as the kernel, they share the same attack surface and can be bypassed once the kernel is compromised. Isolation-based security approaches provide stronger protection by separating security logic from the kernel, but strict isolation often introduces semantic gaps that limit system visibility and hinder timely threat detection. In this paper, we present LOOM, a lightweight out-of-band operating system monitoring architecture built on ARM TrustZone. By leveraging TrustZone's hardware-enforced isolation, LOOM establishes a tamper-resistant monitoring environment independent of the kernel. To bridge the semantic gap, we design a lightweight semantic reconstruction mechanism in the Secure World. It selectively captures the states and behavioral patterns of critical kernel objects, such as process control blocks and kernel modules. Additionally, LOOM introduces a dual-stage hazard prevention mechanism that combines atomic memory protection with an interrupt-driven adaptive agent to detect and mitigate kernel rootkit activities. An address translation cache is further incorporated to optimize repeated address access and reduce monitoring overhead. Overall, we develop a multi-layered collaborative architecture with platform, functional, and auxiliary layers for secure and efficient kernel monitoring. A prototype of LOOM has been implemented on the Phytium D2000 platform. Experimental results indicate that LOOM incurs negligible overhead while maintaining a strong monitoring capability. Furthermore, a security capability analysis based on CVE cases demonstrates that LOOM can detect and mitigate various kernel attacks.

title: Masculinities and Transition in Turkey: Country Brief
abstract: Despite a progressive legal framework and social and human resources policies aimed at benefiting women in Turkey, their labour force participation has remained low. International partners and financial institutions have increasingly focused on promoting an equal opportunities approach to employment and the economy, with a proactive focus on women’s inclusion and advancement. Female entrepreneurship has become seen as a solution to increasing women’s role in the economy, whilst the role of men has typically not been factored into this. An emerging body of research is revealing men’s changing expectations and experiences of shifting gender relations. While less authoritarian ideals of masculinity have evolved among certain groups of Turkish men in recent decades, many remain conflicted and unable to let go of the comforts and benefits of deeply embedded male privileges. This brief is based on a larger study (that also includes Egypt, Kazakhstan and Ukraine), which explores how transition in different countries has been experienced by different groups of men, and its impacts on gender relations. It aims to assist the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and other stakeholders to consider ways of engaging men as agents of positive change for gender equality – alongside women and girls – as well as to complement women-focused projects and investments to enhance both the resilience of transitions and equality of opportunity.

title: Dyna-Think: Synergizing Reasoning, Acting, and World Model Simulation in AI Agents
abstract: Recent progress in reasoning with large language models (LLMs), such as DeepSeek-R1, demonstrates impressive capabilities in domains like mathematics and coding, by exhibiting complex cognitive behaviors such as verification, goal decomposition, and self-reflection. However, it is unclear what behavior is effective and what behavior is missing for long-horizon AI agents tasks. In this work, we propose Dyna-Think, a thinking framework that integrates planning with an internal world model with reasoning and acting to enhance AI agent performance. To enable Dyna-Think, we propose Dyna-Think Imitation Learning (DIT) and Dyna-Think Dyna Training (DDT). To initialize a policy with Dyna-Think, DIT reconstructs the thinking process of R1 to focus on performing world model simulation relevant to the proposed (and planned) action, and trains the policy using this reconstructed data. To enhance Dyna-Think, DDT uses a two-stage training process to first improve the agent's world modeling ability via objectives such as state prediction or critique generation, and then improve the agent's action via policy training. We evaluate our methods on OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena, and demonstrate that Dyna-Think improves the agent's in-domain and out-of-domain performance, achieving similar best-of-n performance compared to R1 while generating 2x less tokens on average. Our extensive empirical studies reveal that 1) using critique generation for world model training is effective to improve policy performance; and 2) AI agents with better performance correlate with better world modeling abilities. We believe our results suggest a promising research direction to integrate world model simulation into AI agents to enhance their reasoning, planning, and acting capabilities.

title: Counterplanning from the Classroom
abstract: In 2013, we formed the Feminist Art and Architecture Collaborative (FAAC), a research group committed to revisiting the art and architectural history survey course with a feminist approach to both content and pedagogy.1 Our aim was to advance the critical approach of “contestation,” which we understand as a constant, open-ended debate and an active, conscious inversion of the power relations that have shaped the value judgments of our disciplines. In doing so, we sought to elide the logic of the canon as a relatively stable roster of names and greatest hits. This proved no small feat: we wanted our process to be practical and implementable in today's university, and, at the same time, we wanted our syllabus to serve as a corrective to the problems we see facing that system.In a moment when higher education is still a major site of inequality, we wondered, is a true “pedagogy of the oppressed” even possible?2 Beyond foregrounding constructions of class, race, and gender at the level of content, could our course also test the boundaries and hierarchies of current teaching methods? In the process, we found ourselves revisiting fundamental questions about how to write history. We agreed that simply adding women and minorities into the canon was not a satisfying solution. Instead, we targeted the frameworks that shape the survey course so that the syllabus would inevitably privilege different kinds of objects and actors. Thus, instead of engaging with monuments and masterpieces, reinforcing the centrality of white male authors, we decided to rethink our categories and replaced these iconic “buildings” (masterpieces or monuments) with “space,” clearing room, as it were, for vernaculars, interiors, and social spaces. The implications of these teaching approaches, we argue, go beyond the classroom and call for new models of scholarship and historiography. Like Silvia Federici and Nicole Cox, who envisioned in their 1975 essay Counter-planning from the Kitchen a feminist, anticapitalist struggle “starting from our kitchens,” we counterplan from the classroom.3The course we designed, Contested Spaces: Art, Architecture, and Politics, traces the construction of modernity around key spaces, objects, and sites of struggle: the plantation, the museum, the school, the prison, the kitchen, the closet, and the urban slum.4 The lectures eschew the pedagogical paradigm that would have students master the canonical narratives of art and architecture in introductory coursework before moving on to revisionist histories. Instead, we posit space, and its representation, as a category from the outset, produced by struggles over power and difference that are not tied exclusively to modernity. In effect, the course takes the form of a forum—a space of public exchange and debate—that we frame with Hannah Arendt's writings on the gendered divide between “polis” and “household” and Nancy Fraser's subaltern counterpublics.5 Thus constituted as a space for discussion, the first half of the course focuses on ideas of othering and the resistance against them, guided in particular by W. E. B. Du Bois's and Silvia Federici's critiques of Marxist thought and by Judith Butler's thoughts on the performativity of gender.6 The second half brings together Michel Foucault's work on institutions and disciplinary power with Angela Davis's and Michelle Alexander's scholarship on the prison–industrial complex.7 Our course narrative concludes with conversations on the possibilities and challenges of protest and dissent.We think of our syllabus as a positive manifesto for a more collective approach to both teaching and scholarship. In this sense, our project resonates with art practices of the 1960s and 1970s, when artists such as Mierle Laderman Ukeles began to criticize the institutional structures that support, display, and promote art.8 Much as Ukeles's Manifesto for Maintenance Art 1969! insistently revalued the invisible labor so often performed by women and workers behind the scenes of cultural institutions like the museum, our syllabus is designed to bring to the surface the invisible power structures and struggles that produce architectural space and construct aesthetic experience. In this way, we seek to reinstate disenfranchised, silenced, and marginalized voices as powerful agents of change and key actors in the construction of modernity.This methodology has had a powerful impact on our scholarship. It has pushed us to examine the value systems that shaped the narratives already available to us and challenged us to think more deeply about the methods for subverting them. Moreover, we have come to realize some of the enormous benefits of the shared production of knowledge, such as the amplification of our knowledge base and the compensation for any singular deficiency. Resisting proprietary models of monadic scholarship and individualized research, we do our work collaboratively.Why art and architecture? Our cross-disciplinary collaboration started fortuitously. We came together as two art historians and two architecture historians motivated to take action on similar exclusions from the standard curriculum and challenge established canons within our respective disciplines. Joining forces compels us to break out of our disciplines’ limitations and forge new paradigms generated by the productive frictions between our fields. Setting the built environment into conversation with art objects helps us highlight architecture's symbolic and affective addresses. Likewise, supplementing our analysis of artworks with an exploration of the “real spaces” they engage allows us to underscore art's real-world implications. For instance, we discuss the symbolic significance of feminine labor in collective kitchens from the Soviet Union to the northeastern United States, while paying heed to the important role kitchen space has played in grounding a network of familial relationships, as framed by the photographs of Carrie Mae Weems. Similarly, the work of Kara Walker allows us to explore the plantation as an affective space in addition to a building typology, as we map out the spatial networks of the transatlantic slave trade and the economies of black and white workers in the southern United States. The interdisciplinary net we cast also pulls into our purview the many contemporary projects that operate at the intersection of art, architecture, and social or urban planning—such as Hélio Oiticica's Penetráveis and Rick Lowe's Project Row Houses—allowing us to emphasize possibilities for art and artists to expand their influence beyond the gallery. Art history thus gains from architectural history an ability to set its objects into larger, dynamic, spatial networks; meanwhile, architectural history relearns the potential of imaginative thought as a political gesture.The resistance to individual authorship that drives our working process also informs our consideration of history—specifically, of the individualistic and proprietary heuristics that shape both art and architecture. The building is most easily enshrined in history either in its idealized form, put forward on the drawing board, or in its final form upon the completion of the transaction and delivery to the client. Similarly, art history still persists in privileging the genius of the singular author, constructing its model of “greatness” around biographical parameters that are most likely to characterize white men's career trajectories (youthful promise, early access to art education, no interruptions in productivity for childbearing, and so forth).9 Such approaches trivialize and simplify the ways art is actually made and the built environment is actually produced. In art and architecture, these approaches treat the social implications of buildings and objects as abstract programs issuing from the intentions of the artists or architects uniquely equipped with the genius to translate them into form. This transactional and episodic logic undermines the longer lives of buildings and objects, either consigning the processes that shape them to oblivion or assuming that they are the outcomes of the authors’ intentions. Narratives of contestation foreground the contingent nature of these processes and bring to history the longer life of art and architecture, along with the diverse actors who have contributed to them.The tendency simply to follow professional(ized) actors in both fields privileges agents who had access to education while doubly excluding those who did not, first by obfuscating the historically white supremacist and patriarchal nature of art and architectural education, and second by denying a place in history to those women, people of color, workers, and others who have always created art and shaped space in spite of exclusion. Such accounts will necessarily skip over the artistic productions of the enslaved, such as the stoneware vessels inscribed with original verse that Dave Drake (also known as Dave the Potter) produced while enslaved in South Carolina, as well as the architectural proposals made by Melusina Fay Peirce and other “housewives of Harvard Square” in the 1860s for cooperative housework societies that would alter the shape of domestic labor.10 The desire to include such actors has pushed us to rethink not only the objectives of the syllabus—what it is that we want our students to learn about the built environment and art—but also its structure and form. We assign scholarship that places the dialectical and often conflictual processes that shape space—as opposed to the innovations of individuals—front and center. The concept of “contestation” challenges professors, students, and scholars alike to seek out and account for the moments when disenfranchised actors and their roles become visible and palpable.Even as our disciplines seek to expand beyond Eurocentric curricula, we remain concerned that our fields continue to follow the trails of capitalist and imperialist power. As capital moves, it carries with it the structures of oppression that it needs to operate. Any global history of art or architecture that uses the pathways of power and capital as the narrative thread that binds its objects together reproduces and reifies the same patterns it seeks to undermine. In their efforts to denounce the long reach of empire, for example, such histories tend to leave out important instances of resistance. They also inevitably retain blind spots with regard to the contributions of historical actors who did not originally hold the reins of power. Our approach to history forces the historian to grapple with the ways capitalism has shaped the temporal and geographic parameters of current histories of art and the built environment. Histories that look to art and architecture as the products of power struggles are more dynamic. They lend themselves to intersectional analyses capable of decentering the logic of capital and apprehending class, gender, and race as forces that have shaped the spaces we live in, the objects we produce, and the ideas we imagine.In fall 2016 we put the syllabus to the test, teaching it at the same time at Bard College, Michigan State University, and the University of Michigan. Always in communication with one another, each instructor organized her own classroom, with students getting a glimpse into the multiple narratives and scholarly approaches through a shared website.11 Our collaboration model for students—the next generation of architects and historians in particular, but also the next generation of citizens—was meant to inspire new ways of thinking about art and architecture, the writing of history, the learning process, and the framing of research. But it also invited them into collaboration with their peers and with their instructors. In weekly report assignments, students reviewed the material from the prior week's unit, building a narrative of their accomplishments, creations, and debates for an outside audience—their “virtual classmates,” as they began calling each other. At the same time, the course structure opposed the position of the teacher as an unchallenged authority figure. The traditional model of the solo-instructor classroom lends itself to what Marxist pedagogue Paulo Freire has called a “banking” model of education, whereby a single expert, standing at the head of the classroom (usually a lecture hall), “deposits” ready-made information and knowledge into the minds of the students, who are positioned, argues Freire, as receptive “containers.”12 Countering this model, multiple instructors and weekly dispatches between campuses produced a multitude of critical approaches to each topic, denying any one narrative singular importance.Over the course of the semester, we used the form of the class to make our students aware of both the processes of contestation that have produced contemporary institutions and, even more important, the conditions of their own education. Besides being the topic of one of the units in Contested Spaces, “school” is the subtextual topic of every unit of the course. Teaching and learning collaboratively across campuses expanded our students’ classrooms and broke down institutional bubbles, offering a weekly glimpse into the work being done on other campuses. This “expanded classroom” challenged our students to see that college is not a static and homogeneous formation, but rather an institutionally specific educational experience structured by concrete, knowable, yet varying economic conditions, departmental and institutional policies, and geographic realities. Students’ metacognition of their learning experience pushed them to form solidarities with one another around their educational conditions but also to be more active, aware, and alert participants in their own educations and on their own campuses.By and large, in academia research is seen and valued as “productive” labor, while teaching is seen as a secondary form of reproductive labor. Teaching is coded by capitalism as merely reproductive, feminized and treated as secondary in importance to what are taken to be more primary forms of knowledge production. We understand this binary to be deeply encoded in the still patriarchal remunerative structures of academe that position us all; our Contested Spaces course critiques and challenges this notion. We take educating the next generation of scholars, thinkers, and citizens to be a form of knowledge production equivalent to and continuous with our scholarship. We hope that the increased awareness our students gain from our class will prompt them to intervene and fight for more just spaces in their worlds. Canon is a noun, but contesting is a verb and an action.

title: AI-powered agent workflows for collaborative learning: addressing educational challenges in the age of artificial intelligence
abstract: Los estudiantes universitarios modernos utilizan habitualmente tres o más herramientas de inteligencia artificial (IA) de forma simultánea — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, GitHub Copilot, entre otras — pero ninguna de estas herramientas comparte memoria ni contexto entre sesiones ni entre miembros de un mismo equipo. Esta fragmentación produce una pérdida de contexto sistemática que obliga a los usuarios a reconstruir manualmente el estado de trabajo cada vez que cambian de modelo o de sesión. En entornos de trabajo colaborativo, el problema se amplifica: cada miembro del equipo opera con una instancia de IA aislada, sin acceso al historial ni al contexto generado por sus compañeros. Este Trabajo de Fin de Máster investiga la naturaleza y el impacto de esta fragmentación mediante un estudio empírico de 21 entrevistas semiestructuradas realizadas en el START Summit de St. Gallen (Suiza) en marzo de 2026, siguiendo el protocolo Mom Test para minimizar el sesgo del investigador. Los participantes eran estudiantes de posgrado, investigadores y profesionales técnicos de nueve países. El análisis temático inductivo de los datos identificó seis patrones recurrentes: fragmentación universal de herramientas de IA (21/21 participantes), pérdida de contexto como principal punto de fricción (17/21), ausencia de memoria de IA compartida en equipos (14/21), bloqueo de contexto por dependencia de modelo (15/21), confusión en la selección de modelos (8/21), y violaciones de atribución de código en herramientas de codificación agéntica (5/21). En respuesta a estos hallazgos, el trabajo presenta el diseño, implementación y evaluación de UniHiveX, un espacio de trabajo colaborativo con IA que incorpora memoria persistente compartida, portabilidad de contexto entre modelos y colaboración a nivel de equipo. El sistema está implementado sobre React, Supabase y Azure, con integración de múltiples modelos de lenguaje de gran escala (GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.7, Grok). La evaluación se realizó mediante un estudio controlado con n=31 estudiantes del Máster en Ingeniería del Software de la UPM el 25 de mayo de 2026. Los resultados muestran que el 87% de los estudiantes pudo contribuir activamente al espacio de trabajo compartido (media H1: 3,95/5, SD=0,82), con 573 llamadas a agentes registradas en 11 equipos. La hipótesis H1 sobre coordinación mejorada en espacio compartido fue respaldada; H2 sobre consistencia de salidas de IA obtuvo respaldo parcial, identificando áreas de mejora en la relevancia contextual de los agentes. Este trabajo realiza cuatro contribuciones al campo: (1) una caracterización empírica de la fragmentación del contexto de IA como clase de ruptura colaborativa; (2) un conjunto validado de ocho requisitos de diseño derivados inductivamente; (3) un artefacto de sistema implementado y evaluado en condiciones reales; y (4) un conjunto de datos cualitativos y cuantitativos que fundamenta el diseño del sistema. --ABSTRACT-- University students routinely use three or more artificial intelligence tools simultaneously — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, GitHub Copilot, and others — but none of these tools share memory or context across sessions or team members. This fragmentation produces systematic context loss, requiring users to manually reconstruct working state whenever they switch models or return to a task. In collaborative settings, the problem is compounded: each team member operates with an isolated AI instance, unable to access the history or context generated by colleagues. This Master's Final Project investigates the nature and impact of this fragmentation through an empirical study of 21 semi-structured interviews conducted at START Summit St. Gallen, Switzerland in March 19-20, 2026, following Mom Test protocol to minimize researcher bias. Participants included graduate students, researchers and technical professionals from nine countries. Inductive thematic analysis identified six recurring patterns: universal AI tool fragmentation (21/21 participants), context loss as the primary pain point (17/21), absence of shared team AI memory (14/21), context lock-in through model dependency (15/21), model selection confusion (8/21), and code attribution violations in agentic coding tools (5/21). In response to these findings, this project presents the design, implementation and evaluation of UniHiveX, a collaborative AI workspace incorporating persistent shared memory, cross-model context portability and team-level collaboration. The system is built on React, Supabase and Azure, integrating multiple large language models (GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.7, Grok). Evaluation was conducted through a controlled study with n=31 European Master on Software Engineering students at UPM on May 25, 2026. Results show that 87% of students could actively contribute to the shared workspace (H1 mean: 3.95/5, SD=0.82), with 573 agent calls logged across 11 teams. Hypothesis H1 on improved team coordination in a shared workspace was supported; H2 on AI output consistency received partial support, identifying areas for improvement in agent contextual relevance. This work makes four contributions: (1) an empirical characterization of AI context fragmentation as a class of collaborative breakdown; (2) a validated set of eight design requirements derived inductively from the data; (3) an implemented system artefact evaluated under real-world conditions; and (4) a qualitative and quantitative dataset grounding the system design.

title: Leveraging Large Language Model for Heterogeneous Ad Hoc Teamwork Collaboration
abstract: Compared with the widely investigated homogeneous multi-robot collaboration, heterogeneous robots with different capabilities can provide a more efficient and flexible collaboration for more complex tasks. In this paper, we consider a more challenging heterogeneous ad hoc teamwork collaboration problem where an ad hoc robot joins an existing heterogeneous team for a shared goal. Specifically, the ad hoc robot collaborates with unknown teammates without prior coordination, and it is expected to generate an appropriate cooperation policy to improve the efficiency of the whole team. To solve this challenging problem, we leverage the remarkable potential of the large language model (LLM) to establish a decentralized heterogeneous ad hoc teamwork collaboration framework that focuses on generating reasonable policy for an ad hoc robot to collaborate with original heterogeneous teammates. A training-free hierarchical dynamic planner is developed using the LLM together with the newly proposed Interactive Reflection of Thoughts (IRoT) method for the ad hoc agent to adapt to different teams. We also build a benchmark testing dataset to evaluate the proposed framework in the heterogeneous ad hoc multi-agent tidying-up task. Extensive comparison and ablation experiments are conducted in the benchmark to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. We have also employed the proposed framework in physical robots in a real-world scenario. The experimental videos can be found at https://youtu.be/wHYP5T2WIp0.

title: Nurturing a new generation of geographers
abstract: The first week of July was a busy time for those attending the Institute of Australian Geographers’ conference in Adelaide, South Australia. Like all such meetings of our community I have attended, it was characterised by collegial warmth, interesting presentations, and opportunities to mingle during breaks, social events, and field trips. Huge thanks to the organisers and Council for your efforts. Later in the week, Iain Hay powerfully appealed to us all to understand the parlous state of the discipline in Australia and to be strong public advocates for what we do, including across all three tiers of government and the private and non-government sectors. His views will feature in our Wiley Lecture paper in due course. I mention that important presentation because, early in the week, I was delighted to spend part of an afternoon with around 40 higher degree research candidates in a conversation focused on writing and publishing strategies. If their penetrating questions and engaging discussions are anything to go by, I have hope for geography—notwithstanding the perennial and urgent need to ensure the discipline is visible, legible, and relevant to those who shape policy across all sectors. With their blessing, I want to share the questions higher degree research candidates had prepared in advance and which I was provided in the lunch break to reflect on prior to our session. Their queries reveal both concerns our early career peers have and their views on the state of the discipline and higher education and on writing and publishing (see also Stratford, 2024; Stratford et al., 2024). The questions illuminate a collective astuteness that bodes well, especially IF more of us energetically campaign for geography in the public domain to optimise the chance, first, that the discipline is recognised and funded under its own name and, second, that new job opportunities are created from those efforts. What I won’t do here is provide the answers I worked through with the candidates. Doing so would turn this work into a longer paper rather than an editorial and perhaps in the new year I can return to such a task. In the interim, readers might be interested in viewing one of our webinars from February this year on a related topic. You can find the recording on the journal homepage under Browse > Webinars. Last but not least, I am delighted to welcome to the core editorial team two new Associate Editors, Brian Cook and Miriam Williams. My thanks to them for their engagement and service. And thanks, too, to Mark Wang, who is stepping down from the Board. I also want to welcome Sarah Rogers and Catherine Walker, who are joining the Board from mid-year. We are always deeply grateful to Board members, reviewers, authors, and our readers for ongoing support for the journal, discipline, and Institute and I know our colleagues at Wiley feel the same. [Correction added on 9 July 2024, after first online publication: Last paragraph in section 1 has been added] This issue leads with Associate Editor Clare Mouat’s observations on the labours of decolonisation and regeneration by grassroot and geography communities, and builds on last year’s commentary by her in its focus on the revolutionary possibilities of love as wayfinding (Mouat, 2023). On this occasion, Mouat (2024) shares her views on Matariki (aka Pleiades), which marks a ‘Māori new year holiday, unifying national identity, and sky-sharing across intersecting knowledge systems’. We then feature another in our running series of special commentaries on COVID-19, in which Somaiah et al. (2024) consider challenges faced by migrant domestic workers and transnational foodcare chains in pandemic times. Their focus is on Southeast Asia and the vital foodwork women engaged in during the emergency, and the conclusion is telling: ‘foodcare chains have proven to be resilient so far, pressures on long-term remittance-driven maternal migration into precarious work are likely to intensify with prolonged crisis’. The balance of the issue comprises eight original papers. The first four all concern matters broadly pertaining to urban environments but from diverse places around the globe and drawing on divergent perspectives to provide a range of novel insights. Hsu et al. (2024) share new research on co-working office spaces in Sydney and critically examine a range of spatiotemporal dynamics and industry patterns evident in their analysis. They establish that there is a growing trend across industry types to provide co-working office space for spatial flexibility, and show how co-working spaces are increasingly concentrated in urban office landscapes within the CBD and emerging throughout the city. In work by Boswell et al. (2024), the politics of do-it-yourself urbanism are considered in terms of experimentation, privilege, and difference. Their focus is the post-quake DIY urban venue, Pallet Pavilion, in Christchurch, Aotearoa New Zealand. Their analysis of its effects shows both the potential for gentrification and a radical city politics based around creating spaces for difference. Then, Legacy et al. (2024) provide a forensic exploration of transport planning history in Victoria, Australia, and propose an alternative transport planning practice grounded in an ethics of care that has salience well beyond the case. Kanosvamhira and Tevera (2024) then unveil their work on quiet activism in urban community gardens, showing how those sites are powerful and liberatory agents for food sovereignty both in general and in South Africa, where their work is based. Flowing logically—at least in my eyes—from that paper is another focused on rural and regional communities, work by Wu et al. (2024) on how Timorese seasonal workers in Australia experience isolation and opportunity and craft third spaces, with at least some such experiences being inflected with colonialist undertones. As I curated the issue, that observation on my part led me to position next a paper by Chen and Howitt (2024) entitled Taiwan inside-out: rescaling colonial constructions of Taiwan through a Tayal-focused lens. Where many works on this fascinating archipelago consider it in relation to mainland China, this one engages in ‘refocusing a scaled geopolitical lens on Indigenous Tayal people of northern Taiwan … [to offer] new perspectives on the social construction of scale and wider geopolitics’ and turns ‘thinking about Taiwan inside-out’. The seventh and eighth papers in the issue deal with particular cohorts and their geographies. In one, Taylor et al. (2024) outline work on the Healthy Ageing/Vulnerable Environment (HAVEN) Index. Combining data about social, economic, and built and physical environments, it helps identify areas associated with higher risk of mortality and emergency morbidities among older people—in this instance, in Adelaide, South Australia. And last, Mansvelt (2024) has written a richly storied account of hosting and the normative presence of Christmas in older people’s lives. That work touches on how the Christmas season reflects and creates powerful social norms that shape a range of socialities, subjectivities, and spatialities, which Mansvelt considers in detail to reveal their wider relevance in broadly Christian cultures. Last but not least, we have two book reviews for your information. The first by Burton (2024) centres on Greg Sharzer’s (2022) Late escapism and contemporary neoliberalism: alienation, work and utopia; the second by Feng Kong (2024) on Amrita Daniere and Matthias Garschagen’s (2019) book, Urban climate resilience in Southeast Asia. Enjoy—and do remember, if you have recently published a book or read something and would like to provide a review, please let us know.

title: Position Paper: Bounded Alignment: What (Not) To Expect From AGI Agents
abstract: The issues of AI risk and AI safety are becoming critical as the prospect of artificial general intelligence (AGI) looms larger. The emergence of extremely large and capable generative models has led to alarming predictions and created a stir from boardrooms to legislatures. As a result, AI alignment has emerged as one of the most important areas in AI research. The goal of this position paper is to argue that the currently dominant vision of AGI in the AI and machine learning (AI/ML) community needs to evolve, and that expectations and metrics for its safety must be informed much more by our understanding of the only existing instance of general intelligence, i.e., the intelligence found in animals, and especially in humans. This change in perspective will lead to a more realistic view of the technology, and allow for better policy decisions.

title: GeoNatureAgent (GNA): A Framework and Benchmark for Pre-Production Evaluation of Tool-Using Agents on Geospatial and Environmental Tasks
abstract: Before tool-using LLM agents are deployed in environmental and geospatial workflows, teams need evidence that an agent reliably selects the right operations against real APIs. We introduce GeoNatureAgent (GNA), a framework for pre-production evaluation of tool-using agents: a fixed sixteen-tool geospatial interface published as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, so the agent under test is the only variable, scored against an identical tool layer, task suite, and deterministic scorer. Its flagship instance is a 103-task benchmark (a 93-task main suite across 18 categories plus a ten-task comparison expansion) evaluated against an open, self-hostable geospatial API serving three environmental indicators across Spain and Portugal. We evaluate nine LLMs under three temperature-1.0 seeds, reporting capability and per-case cost as orthogonal axes. (1) Claude Sonnet 4 achieves the highest capability (61.7% +/- 0.7% on all 103 tasks; 60.8% on the main suite), followed closely by DeepSeek V3.2 (57.9%), while no other model exceeds 53%; (2) the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier is mostly open-weight, with DeepSeek V3.2 offering 93% of Claude's capability at 11.3x lower list-price cost; (3) under strict all-checks scoring the best model sits 24-36 points below the 85-97% reported on general-purpose GIS benchmarks, whereas per-check partial credit for the top four models (86-90%) is comparable, so much of that gap reflects scoring strictness rather than task difficulty alone. The MCP server, evaluation harness, benchmark, and API are publicly available; swapping the tool executors and task suite instantiates an equivalent benchmark for any geospatial domain.

title: AI for Gender Justice: Innovating Caste and Gender Equity in Digital and Real-World Spaces
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly integral to decision-making across sectors including healthcare, policing, education, and employment.While often celebrated for its neutrality and efficiency, AI systems frequently replicate and exacerbate historical injustices related to caste, gender, and class hierarchies.Particularly in the Indian context, where caste and gender intersect deeply to structure societal privilege and marginalization, AI-driven technologies risk reinforcing systemic inequities unless designed consciously with ethical interventions.This research paper critically examines how biases rooted in caste and gender manifest in AI systems through biased datasets, algorithmic design, and governance failures.Drawing on technofeminism, intersectionality theory, algorithmic fairness frameworks, and original field data from a community survey, this paper argues for an interdisciplinary, justice-driven approach to AI development.By analyzing failures in content moderation, predictive policing, hiring algorithms, and language models, and proposing robust technical and policy recommendations, the study demonstrates that AI innovation must prioritize inclusivity, equity, and accountability to become a true agent of social transformation.

title: Frank Whigham and Wayne A. Rebhorn, eds., The Art of English Poesy by George Puttenham: A Critical EditionThe Art of English Poesy by George Puttenham: A Critical Edition. Edited by Frank Whigham and Wayne A. Rebhorn. Ithaca, NY, and London: Cornell University Press, 2008. Pp. xii+498.

OramSmith College Search for more articles by this author Smith CollegePDFPDF PLUSFull Text Add to favoritesDownload CitationTrack CitationsPermissionsReprints Share onFacebookTwitterLinked InRedditEmailQR Code SectionsMoreThis fine edition of George Puttenham's Art of English Poesie, by Frank Whigham and Wayne A. Rebhorn, presents a modernized, extensively glossed, and annotated text. TheArt is unusually wide-ranging in its interests and references, necessitating a comparable range of inquiry for its editors, and where there is not enough space at the bottom of the page they have added twenty pages of longer notes on topics, from the differences between carol, ballad, song, round, and virelay, to the respective offices of the lord chancellor and the lord keeper, to Anglo-Flemish politics. The edition also provides a long, full, and often brilliant introduction, which sketches Puttenham's biography, rehearses the evidence for his authorship of The Art, describes the cultural materials on which the book draws, analyzes its poetics, and discusses it as an embodiment of its author's ambitions. The introduction develops a double thesis: that the book merges a “poetics and rhetoric manual with the core functions of a courtesy book” (60) and that Puttenham's “literary, social and political ambitions shape practically every aspect” (49) of The Art.Puttenham was born in 1530, the second son of a Hampshire gentry family (and nephew of Sir Thomas Elyot). He matriculated at Cambridge, though he took no degree, and in 1556 became a member of the Middle Temple. In 1559 he married a rich widow, Elizabeth, Lady Windsor, and ceased practicing, except for a series of personal lawsuits. He traveled sporadically on the Continent in the 1560s and probably earlier. He seems to have written a good deal, of which three works survive: Partheniades (1579), a single manuscript of poems addressed to Queen Elizabeth; a justification of the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots (1586–87) in multiple manuscript copies; and The Art of English Poesie, begun perhaps in the middle 1560s and published anonymously in 1589.Most graduate students know The Art for its vivid Englishing of Greek and Latin rhetorical terms—”Ironia, or the Dry Mock,” “Sarcasmus, or the Bitter Taunt,” “Hyperbole, or the Overreacher.” But Puttenham's intelligent book offers an extensive account of poetry and rhetoric. Book 1 develops a defense of poetry and characterizes poetic genres, book 2 treats metrical and stanzaic form, and book 3 deals with language and rhetoric. The great twentieth-century edition of The Art by Gladys Doige Willcock and Alice Walker (Cambridge: University Press, 1936) stressed its author's independence and urbane self-confidence. Some of the Partheniades suggest that he was religiously heterodox, and as a critic he often diverges from tradition. Pace Scaliger, whom he uses extensively, he refused to believe that pastoral was the first genre, and he rejected the usual division of rhetorical figures into schemes (which affect the ordering of words) and tropes (which affect meaning) for a tripartite division of his own.Willcock and Walker stressed that Puttenham saw poetry not simply as a moral agent but as “the expression of the whole range of human interests and needs” (xlii). For him, different genres are “so many varieties of response to the whole gamut of human experience and to all the phases of human evolution” (lvi). (Whigham and Rebhorn build on this foundation in laying out the fine discriminations with which Puttenham treats art and nature.) His linguistic patriotism appears in the history of English poetry ending the first book—probably the first such history to have been written, although William Webbe's A Discourse of English Poetrie (1586) was published earlier. The Art offers remarkably specific comments on particular authors and passages, attending to how words affect the reader through sound, organization, and trope: “His intense, often rather technical concern with poetry means that he really reads what occupies his attention” (lx). Puttenham has a mid-Tudor sensibility, quoting most frequently from Tottel's Miscellany (1557). While The Art never reaches the heights of Sidney's Apology (1595), the book suggests how someone might read poetry before its efflorescence in the last two decades of the sixteenth century.While the new edition builds on the earlier one, it differs radically, not least in what the book teaches. Yet both agree in believing that it reflects its creator. Willcock and Walker admit that “consideration for others was not…Puttenham's strong point” (xxviii), but they nonetheless see him as a freethinking, genially independent soul. Whigham and Rebhorn, by contrast, view the book as the work of “an injured, bellicose and, it must be said, vicious nature” (7). Their judgment derives in part from archival materials to which Willcock and Walker had no access and which have been deployed persuasively by Steven W. May in “George Puttenham's Lewd and Illicit Career” (Texas Studies in Literature and Language 50 [2008]: 143–76). They suggest that Puttenham was a sociopath incapable of keeping his word and given to assault, adultery, rape, and spousal abuse—so much so that when his wife sued for divorce, she actually obtained it from the Court of Arches. Puttenham consistently refused to pay the alimony that the courts granted her, and his evasions of these and other debts made the last fifteen years of his life largely an alternation between imprisonment and hiding from the law. His wife's mistreatment eventually came before the Privy Council, and May argues that he published The Art anonymously because of the opprobrium attached to his name. The introduction comments that he “seems to have combined great intellectual acumen with the worst features of character” (60).For Whigham and Rebhorn, the book finally concerns itself with self-promotion at court in two senses. First, as detailed in Whigham's Ambition and Privilege: The Social Tropes of Elizabethan Courtesy Theory (1984) or Daniel Javitch's Poetry and Courtliness in Renaissance England (1978), the account of poetic language implicitly gives would-be courtiers models for how to move (in Puttenham's words) “from the cart to the school, and from thence to the court” (378). “Qui nescit dissimulare nescit regnare,” he quotes as he introduces “allegoria, or the figure of false semblant” (271), suggesting that poetic indirections image a king's or a courtier's duplicity. The introduction shrewdly points out that Puttenham's English versions of rhetorical terms effectively make them into allegorical figures. “He transforms the vast majority of tropes and schemes into characters : etiologia becomes ‘the Tell-Cause.’…Sometimes the personifications seem to identify actual social types, as when protocatalepsis is turned into ‘the Presumptuous' and hyperbole into ‘the Loud Liar, otherwise the Overreacher’” (59).Second, Puttenham engages in continuous, sometimes dishonest, self-presentation to his readers and especially to his principal reader, the queen. He pretends to more learning than he has and more travel than he has really experienced (51–52), and when he substitutes his own tripartite division of rhetoric for the traditional classification of tropes and schemes, the shift is less radical than it appears, dividing the “schemes” in two and setting them on either side of the tropes. (Yet the editors also point out that this division has independent merit, addressing problems in the traditional twofold classification.) The text possesses an “emotional density” (5) caused by Puttenham's ambivalence toward the necessary humiliations of courtship and toward the queen herself. That ambivalence leaves its traces in the text, and the introduction's most brilliant readings treat particular anecdotes as “dreamwork” (67), meaning more than their author consciously intended.The differences between the two editions of The Art suggest how much one's reading of the tone of an early modern passage depends on what one already believes about its author. In this edition what Willcock and Walker saw as genial and confident independence becomes a mixture of hostility and aggressive self-promotion. The latter certainly seems to agree better with what we now know of Puttenham's life. Yet there are problems with the account of The Art as a courtesy book. To begin with, as a courtier Puttenham was a flop. He did not have the personal court knowledge of a Castiglione. May's article on Puttenham's career points out that he was never a member of the courtly circles he aspired to: his flagrant defiance of the law antagonized precisely the people who might have backed his promotion. To the degree that he gives advice, it is derivative, secondhand advice, the view of an outsider. It embodies, to use a word Whigham and Rebhorn use often, no more than a “fantasy” of advancement.Further, in viewing the book primarily as its author's fantasy of promotion, the editors limit its significance. Bad men do write good books. Willcock and Walker argue convincingly that The Art is the work of more than twenty years, written over several stages, and that it embodies Puttenham's abiding, intelligent interest in poetry, especially the possibilities of English verse. The Art is a long book, and much of it has little to do with courtiership or even with linguistic indirection. The thorough account of sound, metrics, and verse form in the second section, illuminated by this new edition's footnotes, concerns itself with technical poetic matters. Even when Puttenham moves to “allegoria or the figure of faux semblant,” the examples adduced are unexpectedly tame. They are varieties of metaphor, mostly pretty obvious, and not much about them dissembles in the garden-variety sense. “We dissemble after a sort when we speak by common proverbs…as thus: As the old cock crows, so does the chick” (273). “After a sort,” indeed. The stress on dissembling in such unlikely contexts suggests that the author would like to see himself as more devious than he is—an Elizabethan Sir Politic Would-Be. Yet the courtesy-book argument does have real force for the work's last twenty-five pages, especially the final chapter of book 3, where Puttenham describes the decorum of actions, not words.In any event, Whigham and Rebhorn's careful account of all the book's arguments goes beyond their somewhat reductive thesis. Their patient elucidation of this long, rich text makes this the definitive edition of The Art for the foreseeable future.
